persona.name: Maya Okafor
persona.about: Backend engineer who reads about databases and compilers, and follows the energy transition on the side.

articles.author: Ines Varga
articles.title: Why your Postgres planner ignores the index you just built
articles.summary: Statistics, not stubbornness: the planner skipped the new index because its row estimates said a sequential scan was cheaper.
body: A new index that the planner refuses to use is one of the most common surprises in Postgres. The planner is not being stubborn; it compares estimated costs, and those estimates come from table statistics gathered by ANALYZE.

Right after a bulk load the statistics can be stale. The planner then believes the predicate matches far more rows than it does, and a sequential scan looks cheaper than thousands of random index reads.

Running ANALYZE on the table, raising the statistics target for a skewed column, or creating extended statistics for correlated columns usually fixes the estimate. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows estimated and actual rows side by side, which is the fastest way to see the gap.

articles.author: Tomasz Lind
articles.title: B-trees, explained with a library card catalogue
articles.summary: A walk through B-tree pages, splits and fill factor using the drawers of an old card catalogue.
body: Picture a card catalogue: a cabinet of drawers, each labelled with the first and last card inside. You never search every drawer; the labels tell you which one to open. A B-tree works the same way, with internal pages playing the role of drawer labels.
When a drawer is full, the librarian splits it in two and adds a label. B-trees split pages the same way, which keeps the tree shallow: a few levels cover millions of rows.
Fill factor is the space you leave in each drawer for new cards. Leave none and every insert causes a split; leave too much and the cabinet grows larger than it needs to be.

articles.author: Arjun Mehta
articles.title: Loop unrolling is not always a win
articles.summary: Unrolling trades code size for fewer branches; past a point the instruction cache pays for it.
body: Loop unrolling removes branch overhead by repeating the loop body several times per iteration. On small hot loops it often helps, and compilers do it automatically at higher optimisation levels.
The cost is code size. A loop that no longer fits in the instruction cache, or that pushes neighbouring hot code out of it, can run slower than the original.
Measure with real inputs. Profile-guided optimisation lets the compiler unroll only the loops that are actually hot, which is usually better than a global flag.

articles.author: Ines Varga
articles.title: MVCC in one diagram: how readers never block writers
articles.summary: Multi-version concurrency control keeps old row versions around so every transaction sees a consistent snapshot.
body: Under MVCC an update does not overwrite a row in place. It writes a new version and marks the old one as expired by the updating transaction.

Each transaction carries a snapshot: the set of transactions whose changes it may see. A reader simply skips versions that are too new or already expired for its snapshot, so it never waits for a writer.
The price is garbage: expired versions stay until vacuum removes them. Long-running transactions hold back that cleanup, which is why a forgotten open transaction can make a busy table grow.

articles.author: Sofia Brandt
articles.title: What a battery does on a grid that already has plenty of solar
articles.summary: Grid batteries earn their keep by shifting midday solar into the evening peak and by reacting faster than any power plant.
body: On sunny days, solar output peaks at noon while demand peaks after sunset. Batteries charge in the middle of the day and discharge into the evening, flattening the gap.
They also respond in milliseconds, which makes them good at frequency regulation, a service that used to come from spinning turbines.
The economics depend on the spread between cheap midday prices and expensive evening prices, and that spread narrows as more batteries join the grid.

articles.author: Lea Hoffmann
articles.title: A gentle introduction to SSA form
articles.summary: Static single assignment gives every value exactly one definition, which makes many optimisations simple.
body: In SSA form each variable is assigned exactly once. Where control flow merges, a phi node chooses which incoming definition to use.
That single-definition property makes data flow explicit. Constant propagation, dead code elimination and value numbering become straightforward walks over def-use chains.
Most modern compilers convert to SSA early and leave it late. The phi nodes disappear during register allocation, when values finally get assigned to machine registers.

articles.author: Rosa Delgado
articles.title: Ten tomato varieties that survive a cold spring
articles.summary: Short-season tomatoes for gardens where the last frost comes late.
body: Not every tomato needs a long, hot summer. Short-season varieties set fruit in cooler nights and ripen weeks earlier.
Start seeds indoors six weeks before the last frost, harden the seedlings off gradually, and plant them deep so the buried stem grows extra roots.
Cherry types are the most forgiving. Larger slicing tomatoes need a warm wall or a cloche to ripen before autumn.

articles.author: Tomasz Lind
articles.title: Write-ahead logging: the promise behind every commit
articles.summary: A commit is durable once its log record reaches disk; the data pages can catch up later.
body: Writing every changed page to disk at commit time would be slow and would scatter writes across the disk. Instead, databases append a compact description of the change to the write-ahead log.
Once that log record is safely on disk, the commit is durable. If the server crashes, recovery replays the log to bring the data pages up to date.
The same log feeds replication: a replica that replays the primary's log ends up with the same data.

articles.author: Danny Okoro
articles.title: Our Sunday league's promotion push, week by week
articles.summary: A fictional amateur side's run-in, told through muddy pitches and late equalisers.
body: Six games from the end of the season, the club sat two points off promotion with a squad held together by tape and good humour.
A late equaliser away from home kept the push alive, and a clean sheet the week after put them back in the places.
Whatever happens on the final day, the bar is booked.

articles.author: Arjun Mehta
articles.title: Inlining heuristics, and why they keep changing
articles.summary: Inlining unlocks other optimisations, but deciding when to inline is a cost model full of guesses.
body: Inlining copies a function body into its caller. The call overhead disappears, and more importantly the optimiser can now see both sides of the call at once.
The risk is code growth. Compilers use heuristics based on callee size, call frequency and whether arguments are constants.
Those heuristics change between releases because no single rule works for every program. Profile data makes the decision far less of a guess.

articles.author: Sofia Brandt
articles.title: Interconnectors: sharing wind across borders
articles.summary: High-voltage links between countries let one region's surplus wind cover another's calm day.
body: Weather systems are large but not continental. When one country is calm, a neighbour is often windy.
Interconnectors, usually high-voltage direct current cables, let that surplus flow across borders, which reduces the backup capacity each country needs on its own.
They are slow to build and politically complicated, but each one makes the combined grid steadier.

articles.author: Ines Varga
articles.title: Vacuum, freeze and the transaction ID wraparound you can avoid
articles.summary: Why Postgres must eventually freeze old rows, and how autovacuum settings keep it from becoming an emergency.
body: Postgres transaction IDs are 32-bit counters, so they wrap around. To keep old rows visible after the counter wraps, vacuum marks them frozen: visible to every future transaction.
Autovacuum does this in the background. Trouble starts when it cannot keep up on a large, busy table, or when a long-running transaction stops it from freezing anything.
Monitoring the age of the oldest unfrozen transaction per table, and tuning autovacuum for the biggest tables, turns wraparound from an outage into routine maintenance.

articles.author: Lea Hoffmann
articles.title: Type inference without the mystery
articles.summary: How unification turns a program's constraints into types, explained with a three-line example.
body: Type inference collects constraints from the program: this argument is added to an integer, so it must be an integer; this function is applied to it, so its parameter type must match.
Unification solves those constraints by repeatedly making two types equal, substituting what it learns as it goes.
When the constraints contradict each other, unification fails, and that failure is the type error the programmer sees.

articles.author: Rosa Delgado
articles.title: Composting in a small flat, without the smell
articles.summary: A bokashi bucket and a few rules for composting kitchen scraps in very little space.
body: Bokashi ferments kitchen scraps in a sealed bucket instead of letting them rot in open air, which keeps the smell down.
Layer scraps with the bran, press out the air, and drain the liquid every few days.
After two weeks the fermented scraps can be dug into soil or added to a regular compost bin.

articles.author: Ines Varga
articles.title: Reading EXPLAIN ANALYZE output from the bottom up
articles.summary: Plans execute from the innermost node outwards; start reading where the rows come from.
body: An execution plan is a tree. The innermost nodes produce rows, and each parent consumes rows from its children, so the plan reads from the bottom up.
For each node, compare estimated rows with actual rows. A large gap is usually the root cause of a bad plan, because every decision above it was made on the wrong number.
Loops multiply: a node that runs once per outer row can dominate the total even when each run looks cheap.

articles.author: Tomasz Lind
articles.title: Partial indexes: index only the rows you query
articles.summary: A WHERE clause on an index keeps it small and fast when queries always target a subset.
body: If nearly every query filters on status = 'open', indexing the closed rows wastes space and slows writes.
A partial index includes only rows matching its predicate. It is smaller, stays in cache more easily, and costs nothing on writes to rows outside it.
The planner uses it only when the query's predicate implies the index predicate, so write the query condition the same way.

articles.author: Arjun Mehta
articles.title: Vectorising a loop by hand, then letting the compiler do it
articles.summary: A small loop rewritten with SIMD intrinsics, and the compiler flags that get you most of the way there.
body: SIMD instructions process several values at once. A loop that adds two arrays can add eight floats per instruction instead of one.
Writing intrinsics by hand gives full control but ties the code to one instruction set.
Often the compiler can vectorise the loop itself if it can prove the arrays do not overlap. A restrict qualifier and a look at the optimisation report usually get you most of the speed-up.

articles.author: Sofia Brandt
articles.title: Heat pumps and the winter evening peak
articles.summary: Electrifying heating moves demand onto the coldest evenings; flexibility and insulation decide how hard that peak hits.
body: Heat pumps are far more efficient than gas boilers, but they move heating demand onto the electricity grid, and the coldest evenings are already the busiest.
Pre-heating homes in the afternoon and better insulation spread that demand out.
Planners now model heat pump adoption street by street to see which local transformers will need upgrading first.

articles.author: Lea Hoffmann
articles.title: Algebraic data types for people who write Go
articles.summary: Sum types make invalid states unrepresentable; here is what they look like and how to approximate them.
body: A sum type says a value is exactly one of several shapes: a payment is either a card payment or a bank transfer, never both and never neither.
Pattern matching on sum types lets the compiler check that every case is handled.
Languages without them approximate the idea with interfaces and type switches, which work but cannot prove that every case is covered.

articles.author: Ines Varga
articles.title: Connection pooling: why 500 connections is slower than 50
articles.summary: Each Postgres connection is a process; past a point, more connections mean more contention, not more throughput.
body: Every Postgres connection is a separate backend process with its own memory. Hundreds of them compete for CPU, locks and cache.
Throughput usually peaks at a few times the number of CPU cores. Beyond that, adding connections makes everything slower.
A pooler in front of the database lets thousands of clients share a small, efficient set of server connections.

articles.author: Tomasz Lind
articles.title: LSM trees: why write-heavy databases love them
articles.summary: Log-structured merge trees turn random writes into sequential ones, at the cost of background compaction.
body: An LSM tree buffers writes in memory and flushes them to disk as sorted, immutable files.
Because every flush is sequential, writes are fast even on slow disks. Reads may need to check several files, which Bloom filters keep cheap.
Background compaction merges files to keep reads fast and to drop deleted rows. Tuning compaction is most of the work of running one well.

articles.author: Arjun Mehta
articles.title: Register allocation as graph colouring
articles.summary: Values that are live at the same time interfere; colour the interference graph with as many colours as you have registers.
body: Two values that are live at the same moment cannot share a register. Draw each value as a node and connect the ones that interfere, and you have an interference graph.
Assigning registers is colouring that graph so no connected nodes share a colour. When there are not enough colours, some values are spilled to memory.
Real allocators add heuristics for which values to spill and how to split live ranges, because spills in hot loops are expensive.

articles.author: Sofia Brandt
articles.title: Negative electricity prices, explained
articles.summary: When sunny, windy afternoons meet low demand, generators sometimes pay to keep running.
body: Some power plants are expensive to switch off and on, and some renewables earn subsidies per unit generated. On a sunny, windy, quiet afternoon, supply can exceed demand.
Prices then go negative: generators pay to keep producing because stopping costs more.
Storage and flexible demand, such as charging cars or heating water at those hours, are the market's answer.

articles.author: Lea Hoffmann
articles.title: What a borrow checker actually checks
articles.summary: Ownership and borrowing rules, explained without the folklore.
body: A borrow checker enforces two rules: a value has one owner, and at any time you may have either many readers or one writer, never both.
Those rules rule out data races and use-after-free at compile time.
Most fights with the checker come from holding a borrow longer than needed. Narrowing the scope of a reference usually resolves them.

articles.author: Rosa Delgado
articles.title: Saving seeds from this year's beans
articles.summary: Let a few pods dry on the plant, shell them, and store the seeds somewhere cool and dark.
body: Beans are among the easiest plants to save seed from because they rarely cross-pollinate.
Leave the healthiest pods on the plant until they rattle, then shell and dry the seeds indoors for another week.
Stored cool, dark and dry, they keep for several years.

articles.author: Danny Okoro
articles.title: Final day: promotion decided on goal difference
articles.summary: The fictional Sunday league side's season ends with a nervy afternoon and a lot of checking phones.
body: Level on points going into the last game, everything came down to goal difference.
A three-goal win was needed and arrived in the final minute.
Nobody remembers who scored. Everybody remembers the bar afterwards.

articles.author: Tomasz Lind
articles.title: Covering indexes and index-only scans
articles.summary: If the index holds every column the query needs, the table is never touched.
body: An index-only scan answers a query from the index alone, skipping the table entirely.
It needs every column the query reads to be in the index, either as a key or as an included column, and the visibility map has to show the pages are all-visible.
That second condition is why frequent vacuuming makes index-only scans much more effective.

articles.author: Arjun Mehta
articles.title: Profile-guided optimisation in practice
articles.summary: Feeding real run data back into the compiler: the workflow, the gains, and the pitfalls of stale profiles.
body: Profile-guided optimisation builds the program twice: once with instrumentation to record what actually runs, and again using that profile.
The compiler then lays out hot code together, inlines the calls that matter and unrolls the loops that are actually hot.
The main pitfall is a profile that no longer matches production. Regenerate it whenever the workload changes.

articles.author: Sofia Brandt
articles.title: Why grid connection queues are the real bottleneck
articles.summary: Many finished solar and battery projects wait years for a connection; reforming the queue matters more than new subsidies.
body: Building a solar farm takes months. Connecting it to the grid can take years.
Connection queues are full of speculative projects that reserve capacity they may never use, and every new application waits behind them.
Reforms that require proof of progress, and that study connections in batches, are shortening queues where they have been tried.

articles.author: Ines Varga
articles.title: Choosing between a hash join and a merge join
articles.summary: The planner's choice depends on sort order, memory and row counts; here is how to read its reasoning.
body: A hash join builds a hash table from the smaller input and probes it with the larger one. It needs memory, but no sort order.
A merge join walks two sorted inputs in step. It is cheap when both sides are already sorted, for example by an index.
If the planner picks the wrong one, check the row estimates first, then work_mem, before reaching for planner settings.
